Invited Paper: ShatterQuant: Breaking Uniform Precision
with Block-Wise Mixed-Precision on a Systolic Transformer Hardware Accelerator

Abstract.

Due to limited support for intra-tensor heterogeneous precision in conventional accelerators, neural network quantization remains largely restricted to per-tensor precision assignment. We present ShatterQuant, a hardware-software co-designed framework enabling mixed-precision quantization within each tensor by assigning independent bit-widths to blocks of a weight projection. ShatterQuant couples precision granularity with PE configuration, such that each precision determines an effective block height. We introduce (1) a hardware-aware post-training method that assigns intra-tensor precision based on block-level standard deviation and weight sensitivity; (2) the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator supporting 1/2/4/8-bit weight precision, precision-dependent PE configuration, block rescaling, and integrated softmax and piecewise-linear nonlinearities; and (3) an evaluation of model-hardware tradeoffs using an implementation in the TSMC 16nm PDK operating at 1 GHz, achieving 1.5 TOPS, 760 GOPS/m​m2mm^{2} area efficiency, and 2.8 TOPS/W energy efficiency. On DeiT and ImageNet-1K, ShatterQuant achieves accuracy within 3.3%3.3\% of state-of-the-art mixed-precision techniques while using a 2 bit lower effective bitwidth, while for PixelDiT demonstrates comparable generation quality. ShatterQuant demonstrates how fine-grained intra-tensor mixed-precision can be realized through hardware-software co-design.

1. Introduction

Although transformers (Vaswani and others, 2017) originated in natural language processing, they have become a foundational architecture across many fields, including computer vision (Liu and others, 2021; Touvron and others, 2021; Dosovitskiy and others, 2020) and generative modeling (Peebles and others, 2023; Ma and others, 2024). Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved strong performance in image recognition, while Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have enabled high-quality image generation. However, these improvements come at the cost of substantial computation and memory traffic. Transformer inference repeatedly executes large matrix and attention operations, with diffusion models further amplifying costs by evaluating the transformer backbone across multiple denoising steps (Fournier and others, 2023). Recent efforts to reduce the computational and memory requirements of transformer models have explored a variety of strategies (Navardi and others, 2026), including architecture search (Humes and others, 2026), knowledge distillation, pruning (Kallakuri and others, 2025), and state-space architectures (Aalishah and others, 2026; Lahoti and others, 2026; Hatamizadeh and others, 2026).

Quantization is a promising approach to reduce transformer deployment costs by representing weights and activations using low numerical precision (Zandieh and others, 2026; Cheng and others, 2026; Wang and others, 2025). Uniformly applying low-precision quantization therefore significantly reduces model size, data movement costs, and arithmetic complexity (Geens and others, 2026). However, aggressive quantization, particularly at sub-8-bit widths, often causes unacceptable degradation in classification accuracy or generation quality. In the case of transformers, this is caused by parameters exhibiting nonuniform sensitivity to quantization: different layers, channels, and parameter groups may require different numerical precision. Block-wise quantization addresses this limitation by partitioning tensors into smaller groups that can be independently scaled (Dettmers and others, 2022). Compared with tensor-wise quantization, this finer granularity provides greater representational flexibility, allowing each block to use a scale better suited to its numerical characteristics while enabling more aggressive overall precision reduction.

Despite the advantages of block-wise quantization in retaining accuracy at reduced precision, current inference platforms such as GPUs often struggle to efficiently support mixed-precision blocks due to non-uniform memory accesses and fixed-function compute datapaths. Therefore, in this work, we present ShatterQuant a hardware–software codesign framework for mixed-precision block-wise quantization and inference of transformer models. The framework combines a hardware-aware post-training quantization (PTQ) approach with a custom ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator implemented in TSMC’s 16nm PDK, enabling precision assignments tailored to the accelerator’s hardware characteristics. Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We develop a post-training quantization method for Vision Transformers and Diffusion Transformers that assigns mixed-precision bit widths at the block level, enabling aggressive model compression while preserving for both image classification accuracy and generation quality and evaluate the approach on DeiT ViTs and PixelDiT DiT using Imagenet-1k.

  • •

    We design the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator, which supports 1-, 2-, 4-, and 8-bit integer weights with 8-bit activations. The accelerator couples quantization block size with processing-element (PE) configuration, allowing precision to directly determine effective block dimensions and compute parallelism for joint hardware-software configuration.

  • •

    We implement the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator in TSMC’s 16nm process design kit, directly mapping quantization block sizes to their corresponding PE configurations. We evaluate the resulting design trade-offs in model quality, hardware area, throughput, energy efficiency, and deployment cost across DeiT image classification and PixelDiT image generation on ImageNet-1k.

2. Related Work

2.1. Diffusion Transformers

DiTs replace the convolutional U-Net backbone traditionally used in diffusion models with a transformer architecture, demonstrating that scaling depth, width, and token count leads to improved generative performance while maintaining a simple design (Peebles and others, 2023). Building on this foundation, SiT introduces a scaling strategy that jointly optimizes diffusion training efficiency and sample quality through improved transformer design and training methodologies (Ma and others, 2024). More recently, PixelDiT further improves transformer-based diffusion by operating directly in the pixel domain, eliminating the need for a separate latent autoencoder while maintaining generation quality and scalability (Yu and others, 2026). With the removal of the latent-space autoencoder, we design the ShatterQuant transformer accelerator to focus on the core components of traditional ViT (Dosovitskiy and others, 2020) architectures used in DeiT (Touvron and others, 2021). Specifically, ShatterQuant targets linear projections, attention softmax, and nonlinear activation functions.

2.2. Mixed Precision Quantization

Transformer quantization has emerged as a key technique for reducing the computational and memory costs of large-scale models. GPTQ (Frantar and others, 2023) introduced an effective PTQ framework for transformer weights, enabling low-bit deployment while maintaining high accuracy. Subsequent work has explored quantization-aware training and mixed-precision strategies to better preserve model performance for low-bit vision transformers (Walczak and others, 2025; Wang and others, 2025), improved PTQ through randomized quantization during calibration (Wei and others, 2023), and recent mixed-precision techniques that adapt bitwidths according to layer sensitivity (Hwang and others, 2026; Ranjan and others, 2026; Sun and others, 2026) or explore channel-wise intra-tensor quantization (Byun and others, 2025; Feng and others, 2025). In contrast, ShatterQuant enables grouped sub-channel quantization with dedicated hardware support.

2.3. Hardware Accelerators

Specialized hardware accelerators have become increasingly important for executing transformer workloads by reducing memory movement and accelerating compute-intensive operations. Prior work has explored accelerator designs tailored for low-bit transformer inference (Guo and others, 2025; Lin and others, 2025), including support for hardware-efficient power-of-two quantization and lightweight arithmetic to improve throughput and energy efficiency (Shi and others, 2024; Cho and others, 2025). More recent architectures further optimize transformer execution through specialized mixed-precision dataflows for sparsity (Moon and others, 2026; Zhang and others, 2026), on-chip memory hierarchies, and dedicated support for attention mechanisms and mixed-precision computation (Fang and others, 2025; Cuyckens and others, 2025; Wu and others, 2024; Moghaddasi and others, 2025). These works demonstrate the benefits of hardware-software co-design, but largely rely on coarse-grained precision configurations, exploit sparsity by skipping operations rather than varying the weight precision, or contain limited evaluation on modern transformer architectures.

3. Proposed Approach

The proposed approach, illustrated within Fig. 2, is separated into four subsections: Model Architecture, Intra-Tensor Blockwise Mixed Precision, Post Training Blockwise Quantization, and the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator.

3.1. Model Architecture

The formulation of ShatterQuant begins with the original ViT (Dosovitskiy and others, 2020), which consists of LL transformer layers. A CC-channel input image is partitioned into nn patches, represented as P∈ℝn×(p2⋅C)P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(p^{2}\cdot C)}, and linearly projected into the embedding dimension DD using a learnable projection matrix WE​D∈ℝ(p2​C)×DW_{ED}\in\mathbb{R}^{(p^{2}C)\times D}, concatenated with an optional class token (C​L​SCLS), and have a learned positional embedding added to them, producing the initial token embeddings (XX).

Each transformer layer projects the embeddings XX into queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V) using weights WQ,WK,WV∈ℝD×DW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}:

(1) Q=X​WQ,K=X​WK,V=X​WV.Q=XW_{Q},\qquad K=XW_{K},\qquad V=XW_{V}.

The projections are divided into HH attention heads of dimension dk=D/Hd_{k}=D/H. For each head hh, scaled dot-product attention computes context-aware token representations as

(2) Attnh=softmax⁡(Qh​Kh⊤dk)​Vh,\mathrm{Attn}_{h}=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_{h}K_{h}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V_{h},

The head outputs are concatenated and projected with WO∈ℝD×DW_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}:

(3) Z=Concath=1H⁡(Attnh)​WO∈ℝN×D.Z=\operatorname{Concat}_{h=1}^{H}(\mathrm{Attn}_{h})W_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}.

and processed by a feed-forward network (FFN):

(4) FFN⁡(Z)=σ⁡(Z​W1+b1)​W2+b2,\mathrm{FFN}(Z)=\sigma(ZW_{1}+b_{1})W_{2}+b_{2},

where W1∈ℝD×Df​fW_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D_{ff}}, W2∈ℝDf​f×DW_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{ff}\times D}, Df​fD_{ff} typically set to 4​D4D, with σ\sigma as a nonlinear activation function. Together, these components are coupled with residuals and LayerNorm, defining a single transformer layer as illustrated in Fig. 2.

PixelDiT (Yu and others, 2026) extends the conventional transformer architecture for diffusion-based image denoising by introducing separate patch-wise and pixel-wise transformer pathways. In addition to the standard transformer operations, PixelDiT incorporates adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN), which uses conditioning information to adaptively scale and shift intermediate representations toward the desired class output. Despite these architectural additions, the core transformer computation remains consistent, relying on linear projections and attention operations. We scope our approach applicable to both conventional ViTs and PixelDiT targeting the full attention pipeline and feedforward structure. With this approach we offload operations such as the initial embedding linear and final linear operations, LayerNorm, RoPE, reshaping, and scaling to external processors, while handling the parameterized linear and attention operations on our ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator.

3.2. Intra-Tensor Blockwise Mixed Precision

To formulate the intratensor blockwise mixed precision weights, we first apply tensor-wise AbsMax scaling to the weights, defining β=maxi,j⁡|Wi​j|\beta=\max_{i,j}|W_{ij}| as the weight scale with W~=W/β\tilde{W}=W/\beta. Activations are quantized to a fixed 8-bit range using a tensor-wise scale γ\gamma, initialized at maxi,j⁡|Xi​j|/27\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|/2^{7} and then calibrated to minimize each layer’s output error, while the normalized weights W~\tilde{W} are quantized using block-specific precision and scale. For hardware efficiency, each block scale is constrained to a power of two and represented by a signed 6-bit exponent kr,ck_{r,c} and 2-bit precision br,cb_{r,c}:

(5) sr,c=2kr,c2br,c−1,qmin=−2br,c−1,qmax=2br,c−1−1.s_{r,c}=\frac{2^{k_{r,c}}}{2^{b_{r,c}-1}},\qquad q_{\min}=-2^{b_{r,c}-1},\qquad q_{\max}=2^{b_{r,c}-1}-1.

Writing (r,c)(r,c) for the block containing element (i,j)(i,j), the weights are quantized as

(6) Wi​jmix=clamp⁡(round⁡(W~i​jsr,c),qmin,qmax),Wi​j≈Wi​jmix​sr,c​β.W^{\mathrm{mix}}_{ij}=\mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\mathrm{round}\!\left(\frac{\tilde{W}_{ij}}{s_{r,c}}\right),q_{\min},q_{\max}\right),\qquad W_{ij}\approx W^{\mathrm{mix}}_{ij}s_{r,c}\beta.

As represented in Fig. 2, we make use of non-uniform blocks supporting 8-, 4-, 2-, or 1-bit weights. At 8 bits, each stored weight corresponds to a single output column, while decreasing precision packs two, four, or eight weights, and thus output columns, into the same 8-bit representation. In contrast, activations are quantized to a fixed 8-bit range using the tensor-wise scale γ\gamma:

(7) Xi​jint=clamp⁡(round⁡(Xi​jγ),−128,127),Xi​j≈Xi​jint​γ.X^{\mathrm{int}}_{ij}=\mathrm{clamp}\!\left(\mathrm{round}\!\left(\frac{X_{ij}}{\gamma}\right),-128,127\right),\qquad X_{ij}\approx X^{\mathrm{int}}_{ij}\gamma.

3.3. Post-Training Blockwise Quantization

In order to efficiently quantize pretrained models, we treat each weight block as being part of a “superblock,” where one superblock occupies the same number of weights as a single 1-bit block. Since each block contains a local scale, precisions are determined based on the overall standard deviation (STD) across all superblocks within the selected model using cutoffs within the cumulative distribution function (CDF). As illustrated within stage 1 of Fig. 2, based on the CDF, superblocks with greater STD are coarsely represented using fewer bits, while superblocks with lower STD are represented using higher bitwidths in a fine-grained manner.

To improve model performance we adopt the LS-ViT (Hwang and others, 2026) quantization algorithm, which combines Hessian estimation and reconstruction components (Wei and others, 2023), and we adapt its usage of AdaRound (Nagel and others, 2020) weight rounding to align with the ShatterQuant weight quantization blockwise structure. In addition to AdaRound’s per-weight learned rounding decisions, we extend the weight scaling to the power-of-two block scales kk, as rounding to the nearest power-of-two can result in lost resolution. During layer reconstruction, alongside the per-weight rounding decision variables ui​ju_{ij}, each superblock contains a single vmv_{m} which rounds between 2k2^{k} and 2k−12^{k-1}. Thus, the reconstructed weight is

(8) W^=W^(k)+h⁡(vm)​(W^(k−1)−W^(k)).\hat{W}=\hat{W}^{(k)}+h(v_{m})\left(\hat{W}^{(k-1)}-\hat{W}^{(k)}\right).

Both candidates are fully quantized, so the exponent is selected without relaxing the power-of-two constraint itself, and both decisions are annealed by the same regularizer against the least-squares Hessian objective.

3.3.1. Extension to PixelDiT

We reuse our LS-ViT adaptation for PixelDiT, however, we make several changes. First, we sample a set of image generation trajectories from the full precision model, drawing from multiple classes during the process. We utilize a squared error between the full precision model’s outputs and quantized model’s outputs at each timestep as the task loss for LS-ViT’s Hessian estimation. Second, as prior works (Li and others, 2023) have noted, the activation distributions of diffusion and flow matching models tend to shift over each inference timestep. Therefore, we further extend the LS-ViT adaptation by initially calibrating multiple activation scales per layer, separated into 8 timestep bins, with the active scale selected by timestep. Third, rather than using STD and a CDF-based cutoff, we instead assign precisions via a relative variance score, normalizing each superblock’s variance by the mean variance of its own layer, along with a fixed percent setting a cutoff for the superblocks with greatest relative variance to get high precision, and vice versa. Finally, although we still optimize the per-layer activation scales during reconstruction, we add a post-reconstruction stage which optimizes only the activation scales across all layers to minimize MSE from the FP model trajectories.

3.4. ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator

The ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator architecture is designed to execute transformer workloads aligned with the ShatterQuant quantization method. As shown in Fig. 3, the architecture consists of a weight, scale, bias, and feature input buffers, an 8-bit activation and 1/2/4/8-bit systolic processing array, a 32-bit partial product accumulator, and an integrated quantizer. The accelerator is controlled via a standard AXI-Stream bus for data streaming and AXI-Lite bus for configuration and initialization. We break this architecture down into four subsections: processing element (PE), PE array, output accumulator, and quantizer.

3.4.1. ShatterQuant Processing Element

The ShatterQuant PE represents the lowest level weight-stationary multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) engine capable of supporting 1-, 2-, 4-, and 8-bit weight representation. An integrated barrel rotator with a 2-bit rotation select, dynamically extends and rotates lower-bit weight blocks from the packed 8-bit representation, enabling the same PE to operate across different precision modes while using a unified 8-bit multiplier accumulated into a 32-bit result. For 8-bit weights, the PE performs a standard weight-stationary MAC operation. As precision decreases, the PE exploits increased bit-level serialization by reusing input features across multiple clock cycles. Specifically, 4-bit weights maintain the same input feature stream while generating two output columns over two clock cycles, while 2-bit and 1-bit modes expand this to four and eight output columns, respectively.

3.4.2. ShatterQuant PE Array

For the ShatterQuant PE to support larger matrix sizes at higher throughput, PE’s are tiled across a square p×pp\times p systolic array, with weights and biases propagated down the array, features and weight-precision metadata propagated across, and partial sums accumulated at the bottom into the output accumulator. Since each PE includes a dedicated barrel rotator, an additional weight path enables weight preloading without stalling computation, requiring only a pp clock cycle weight preload latency and 2​p−12p-1 feature clock cycle initial setup latency.

To sustain bandwidth, the weight, bias, and feature buffers are organized with 8×p8\times p-bit-wide interfaces and tunable depths of DWD_{W}, DBD_{B}, and DFD_{F}, respectively. Each scale corresponds to a p×pp\times p block of packed weights; thus, the scale buffer has depth DW/pD_{W}/p, with the two lowest bits encoding the block precision and the six highest bits encoding its scale. This organization establishes a direct relationship between the software block size and the systolic core configuration: as weight precision decreases, the effective processing width expands by a factor of two, increasing the number of output columns computed per cycle.

3.4.3. ShatterQuant Output Accumulator

The output accumulator maintains 32-bit partial sums and incorporates the ShatterQuant rescaler for cross-block accumulation. It comprises of a 32×p32\times p-wide buffer with depth DOD_{O} and an 8-bit-wide column scale buffer with tunable depth DSD_{S}. Rather than dequantizing each block, the rescaling unit adjusts the accumulator scale at block boundaries, enabling integer-domain accumulation. Let ziz_{i} denote the integer partial sum from block ii, with power-of-two scale sis_{i} and corresponding dequantization scale Δi=2si\Delta_{i}=2^{s_{i}} rescaled to the next block’s scale using

(9) O^i+1\displaystyle\hat{O}_{i+1} =(O^i​ΔiΔi+1)+zi+1,\displaystyle=\left(\hat{O}_{i}\frac{\Delta_{i}}{\Delta_{i+1}}\right)+z_{i+1}, ΔiΔi+1\displaystyle\frac{\Delta_{i}}{\Delta_{i+1}} =2si−si+1.\displaystyle=2^{s_{i}-s_{i+1}}.

Thus, rescaling is implemented as a shift by si−si+1s_{i}-s_{i+1}: a positive value applies a right shift, while a negative value applies a left shift with the scale si+1 stored within the column scale buffer for future block rescaling.

3.4.4. ShatterQuant Quantizer

To enable fully integer inference, the accelerator integrates an on-chip quantizer that performs requantization and nonlinear operations without floating-point arithmetic (Dong and others, 2024). This comprises a dedicated max-subtraction tree, piece-wise linear (PWL) approximator, accumulation tree, and Newton–Raphson reciprocal unit (Burkhardt and others, 1981). Because nonlinear inputs originate from the i​n​t​32int32 accumulator, conventional LUT-based implementations are impractical due to their potentially 2322^{32}-entry address space. Instead, the accelerator implements a compact PWL representation (Prasad and others, 2025). Specifically, each function is approximated over a set of input intervals as

(10) f⁡(x)\displaystyle f(x) ≈mn​(x−xn−1)+bn,xn−1≤x<xn,\displaystyle\approx m_{n}(x-x_{n-1})+b_{n},\quad x_{n-1}\leq x<x_{n},

given mnm_{n}, bnb_{n}, and xnx_{n} denote the segment slope, bias, and boundary. The preceding dequantization scales γ​β\gamma\beta and subsequent quantization scale 1/γ′1/\gamma^{\prime} are fused into the PWL slope, such that

(11) mn​γ​βγ′≈sn2κn,\displaystyle m_{n}\frac{\gamma\beta}{\gamma^{\prime}}\approx\frac{s_{n}}{2^{\kappa_{n}}},

where sns_{n} and κn\kappa_{n} are an integer multiplier and power-of-two shift, respectively. The resulting integer approximation is

(12) f^​(x)≈RoundClip⁡((sn​(x^−x^n−1))≫κn+b^n).\displaystyle\hat{f}(x)\approx\mathrm{RoundClip}\left(\left(s_{n}(\hat{x}-\hat{x}_{n-1})\right)\gg\kappa_{n}+\hat{b}_{n}\right).

Each segment requires an i​n​t​32int32 boundary and i​n​t​8int8 scale, shift, and bias, which fuse nonlinearities directly into the requantization stage. For softmax, the quantizer implements the approximation (Zhong and others, 2026)

(13) softmaxI​N​T​8=128​exi−max⁡(x)∑j128​exj−max⁡(x)<<sO,\displaystyle\mathrm{softmax}_{INT8}=\frac{128e^{x_{i}-\max(x)}}{\sum_{j}128e^{x_{j}-\max(x)}}<<s_{O},

where 2sO2^{s_{O}} defines the output scale and 128128 scales the bounded exponential to the i​n​t​8int8 range. The 128128 factor is fused into a PWL approximation of exe^{x}, while sOs_{O} represents a tunable shift on the reciprocal output and serves as the input scale for following layers.

4. Results

We separate evaluation into software and hardware performance, followed by a study of the relationship between accelerator configuration and software performance. ’PE’ is used to describe configurations in both the software and hardware evaluations.

4.1. Model Performance

Focusing on the ability of ShatterQuant to enable intra-tensor blockwise mixed-precision quantization, Fig. 4 summarizes the resulting precision distributions for a 4x4 PE configuration across the three DeiT models using a 5% 1-bit weight target and PixelDiT-XL using 20% 4-bit and 80% 8-bit split. We further compare the resulting effective precision and model accuracy to existing mixed precision approaches in Tab. 1. These results demonstrate ShatterQuant’s ability to assign intra-tensor precisions between 1-8-bit effective precision while maintaining competitive accuracies (maxΔ​3.3%\Delta 3.3\%) compared to coarse-grained per-tensor assignments, with a reduced overall model bitwidth. Applying our technique to PixelDit in Fig.  4 (C) shows ShatterQuant ability to maintain similar image generation capabilities; however, at an increased generative Fréchet Inception Distance (gFID) of 14.4 due to increased quantization noise.

4.2. Hardware Implementation

We implement the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator capable of executing the developed models in SystemVerilog and synthesize it under a TSMC 16nm FinFET technology at 1 GHz. We use a 960 KiB feature, 192 KiB weight, 2 KiB bias, and 256 KiB output buffers synthesized using single-port macros and a quantizer configured with a 16-PWL segment memory and FIFOs capable of storing the required 256 columns during ViT and PixelDiT attention. Power is obtained from gate-level simulation of a representative ViT matmul workload. We evaluate four PE array configurations, 4×\times4 through 32×\times32, obtained by changing the array size alone and modifying the Axi-Stream bus to standard widths of 16, 32, 128, 128 for each configuration, respectively, while holding memory capacity and workload constant. All four configurations meet timing.

The resulting performance breakdowns and the placed layout of the 32×\times32 configuration are presented in Fig. 5. Total area ranges from 1.60 to 1.92 mm2 and power from 64 to 521 mW. The design is memory-dominated. On-chip buffers occupy 86% of the area at 4×\times4 and 79% at 32×\times32, which keeps the area nearly flat until 32×\times32, where the PE array first becomes significant at 13% of area and 40% of power. Power, by contrast, scales with the array throughout. The quantizer, which realizes the INT32–INT8 output activation datapath occupies only 2.6–7.1% of total area.

Comparing the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator with comparable edge-based ASIC accelerators in Tab. 2, ShatterQuant performs at a MAC throughput of 1.5 TOPS with an operating power of 521 mW. Additionally, the ShatterQuant Transformer Accelerator performs at a competitive area and energy efficiency of 760 GOPS/m​m2mm^{2} and 2.8 TOPS/W.

4.3. Hardware-Software Co-Analysis

One of the core traits of ShatterQuant is the correlation between the hardware systolic core configuration and performance with the software model accuracy. To demonstrate this effect, we display the top-1 accuracy for DeiT over the configuration energy efficiency within Fig. 6 for 5 target 1-bit % configurations with the remaining percentages aligning with the CDF assignment method. Compared to the overall model performance, a 0% 1-bit, or an assignment that is primarily dominated by 8-bit weights, leads to the highest performance for all models, approximately <0.5%<0.5\% within the FP model accuracy. As the 1% distribution increases the tiny variant experiences the highest accuracy reduction, reaching approximately 40% at a 4x4 PE configuration. On the other hand, larger models experience a smaller accuracy reduction and a reduced overall model bitwidth, with DeiT-Base reaching 60% at an effective bitwidth of 3-bits. Additionally, as the % of low-precision weights increases, the models experience sharper declines in accuracy and an overall increase in precision as weight-blocks experience finer weight variations. At 32×32 and 20% 1-bit weights, the larger DeiT-Base retains substantially higher accuracy than DeiT-Tiny, indicating greater tolerance to reduced quantization granularity. Thus, larger PE arrays improve energy efficiency at the cost of model accuracy.

We repeat a similar study for PixelDiT; however, due to the highly sensitive nature of diffusion models propagating quantization noise over tens of timesteps, we instead evaluate a higher precision split of 4- and 8-bit weights of 20% and 80%, as shown in Fig. 7. We emphasize the effect of increasing the PE configuration impacting overall model performance by demonstrating a gFiD increase to 50 using a 16x16 configuration, in contrast of a 14 gFiD at a 4x4 configuration using the 20% 4-bit split.

5. Conclusion

This work presented ShatterQuant, a hardware-software co-designed framework for block-wise mixed-precision transformer inference. By jointly optimizing quantization, integer-only execution, and a configurable systolic accelerator supporting dynamic 1/2/4/8-bit computation, ShatterQuant enables efficient deployment of both Vision Transformers and PixelDiT image generation models. Implemented in the TSMC 16nm PDK, ShatterQuant achieves 1.5 TOPS, 760 GOPS/m​m2mm^{2} area efficiency, and 2.8 TOPS/W energy efficiency, while maintaining accuracy within 3.3%3.3\% of state-of-the-art mixed-precision methods on DeiT at a 2-bit lower effective bitwidth, with comparable generation quality on PixelDiT. Together, these results demonstrate that fine-grained intra-tensor mixed-precision quantization can be efficiently realized through hardware-software co-design, improving the performance and flexibility of future transformer accelerators.

Future work will extend mixed-precision quantization to activations and auto-regressive transformers, and explore multi-processor integration (Antonio and others, 2025; Zaruba and others, 2021) to support large machine learning models. Additionally, develop approximations for advanced layers including RoPE positional embeddings, mixture-of-experts, and state-based architectures.
